reason: The run renders one broad sense (deprive of force, put out of operation, bring to an end) with at least six different English expressions: nullify, do away with, abolish, bring to nothing, set aside and render powerless. Some of this variation tracks the object, but without a register nothing keeps it stable. Similar objects are already split: the devil is 'rendered powerless' in Hebrews 2:14 while the lawless one is 'brought to nothing' in 2 Thessalonians 2:8, and the law is 'nullified' in Ephesians 2:15 where tradition has 'abolish'. Several notes in the run also argue against the traditional 'destroy' and 'fading', and that departure needs to be applied uniformly.
sense: to deprive something of force or effect, put it out of operation or bring it to an end; the default governs cases where the object is a law, promise, covenant commitment or the like whose validity is at stake

alternates.when: The object is death, or rule, authority and power as such, brought to an end outright: 1 Corinthians 15:24, 15:26; 2 Timothy 1:10. Use the same word in all three; do not use 'destroy'.
The object is persons or personal beings, or 'the things that are', whose standing is overthrown: 1 Corinthians 1:28, 2:6; 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

Something temporary or provisional is ended or put out of use: 1 Corinthians 6:13; 13:8, 13:10, 13:11; Galatians 5:11. Keep the one rendering for all four occurrences in 1 Corinthians 13:8-11 so the repetition is heard.
2 Corinthians 3:7, 3:11, 3:13, 3:14, of the glory and ministry of the Mosaic covenant and of the veil. Use the same rendering all four times; do not use 'fade'.
The object continues to exist but loses its hold or power: Romans 6:6 (the body of sin) and Hebrews 2:14 (the devil).
Passive with ἀπό, meaning to be discharged or cut off from something: 'released from' the law in Romans 7:2 and 7:6; 'severed from' Christ in Galatians 5:4.
Luke 13:7 only: the barren fig tree making the ground unproductive, the older literal sense of the verb.

traditional: abolish, make void, destroy, do away
rationale: In the usage of the period, and above all in Paul, this verb means to make something idle or inoperative: to take away its force, or to bring it to an end. It is not the ordinary word for destroying, and it does not mean to fade. English has no single word that fits a law, a promise, death, hostile rulers and childish ways alike, so the register fixes one rendering for each kind of object. 'Nullify' is the default for laws and promises, where the question is whether they still hold.
standard_view: The standard lexicons give the senses as: use up or waste (Luke 13:7); make ineffective or nullify; abolish, set aside or bring to an end; and, in the passive with 'from', be released or estranged. Mainstream translations vary the English freely, with 'nullify', 'make void', 'abolish', 'destroy', 'bring to nothing', 'pass away', 'release' and 'sever' all in use. Many have 'destroy' at 1 Corinthians 15:24-26 and Hebrews 2:14. Several have 'fading' for the glory in 2 Corinthians 3; some scholars defend that as a contextual sense, but others reject it as lacking lexical support. Romans 6:6 is divided between 'destroyed', 'done away with' and 'rendered powerless'.
